title: Full-frequency GW from Cayley-transformed self-energy moments
authors: Marcus K. Allen, George H. Booth
abstract: The dynamical GW self-energy approximation is a key computational tool to provide the fundamental spectrum of electronic systems. We reformulate this approximation, representing the particle and hole parts of the GW self-energy through a highly compact set of Cayley-transformed moment constraints. The Cayley transformation maps real frequencies to the unit circle, keeping the moments bounded as their order increases, ensuring numerical stability and allowing resolution to be focused on an energy range of interest. We calculate these Cayley-transformed moments via an efficient O[N$^4$] scaling contour integration, and from them, construct a Hermitian upfolded Hamiltonian with a linearly scaling dimensionality with system size. A single-shot diagonalization of this effective Hamiltonian gives an explicit full-frequency G0W0 Green's function with manifestly real poles and non-negative spectral weights. This enables quasiparticle energies, satellite features, and their spectral weights to be obtained across the full G0W0 spectrum. Comparisons with exact G0W0 calculations and convergence across the GW100 test set and the larger Chlorophyll A molecule demonstrate substantially faster and more reliable convergence with moment order than an earlier monomial-moment approach. These Cayley moment representations therefore provide a stable, compact, and systematically improvable route to the complete spectral information of zero-temperature GW, without explicit frequency grids, plasmon-pole models and other common approximations, or analytic continuation.
summary: This paper introduces a novel method to calculate the full-frequency GW self-energy by reformulating spectral moments using a Cayley transformation. This technique ensures numerical stability and achieves significantly faster convergence compared to prior moment-based approaches. It provides a robust, grid-free route to obtaining complete spectral information for electronic systems.
main_problem: To develop a stable, compact, and systematically improvable method for calculating the full-frequency Green's function ($G_0W_0$) spectrum of electronic systems, overcoming limitations of existing GW approximations.
main_result: The use of Cayley-transformed moment constraints provides a representation that converges substantially faster and more reliably than previous monomial moment approaches, allowing for the calculation of the full spectral information.
method: The authors reformulate the GW self-energy moments using a Cayley transformation, which maps real frequencies to the unit circle. These moments are calculated via efficient contour integration and used to construct and diagonalize a Hermitian upfolded Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to general electronic systems, benchmarked on molecular calculations like Chlorophyll A. The underlying physics involves calculating the $G_0W_0$ self-energy ($\Sigma(\omega)$) within the framework of many-body perturbation theory.
key_observables: Full-frequency $G_0W_0$ Green's function, quasiparticle energies, satellite features, and their spectral weights.
important_parameters: Moment order ($n$), Cayley scale ($\omega_p$), and contour integration parameters ($\sigma$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the ability to compute moments via contour integration and relies on the Cayley map to ensure moment boundedness and numerical stability.
figures_summary: Figures compare the convergence of excitation energies (HOMO/LUMO) using the new Cayley moment expansion (cmGW) versus the old monomial expansion (mGW), showing superior convergence for cmGW. Another figure shows the spectral function of Chlorophyll A for various moment orders.
paper_structure: The paper reviews previous monomial moment expansions, details the calculation of the new Cayley-transformed moments via contour integration, describes implementing Dyson's equation using the moment-conserving upfolded Hamiltonian, and presents convergence results.
why_interesting: The development of highly accurate, non-perturbative spectral methods for electronic structure is crucial for understanding strongly correlated materials where simple approximations fail.
